title: Genesis ends (Genesis 49–50)
hookLine: Jacob's blessings, Joseph's forgiveness, and a coffin waiting to go home; finishing a book, the synagogue says "be strong"
tomorrow: a king who knew not Joseph

cards: A synagogue on a Saturday morning in winter. The Torah scroll lies open on the table, and the reader is chanting the very last verse of Genesis. The whole book, from let there be light to here, is about to be finished.
The moment the last word is sung, the whole room stands and calls out together, three words, loud: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another.
It's a little like the cheer at the end of a long race.

teach.b: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses them one by one. The blessings are honest: some praise, some hard words about old wrongs. He asks to be buried with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah, in Canaan, and he dies.
Joseph and his brothers carry him home with a great Egyptian procession and bury him. Then, walking back to Egypt, the brothers get scared. Now that Father is gone, maybe Joseph will pay us back.
They send him a message, and they fall down before him.

teach.h: AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?
teach.b: Joseph weeps, and says: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God? And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He'll take care of them, and their little ones.

Years of peace after the reunion, and they still needed to hear it again. Sometimes forgiveness has to be said twice. Then Joseph grows old, and asks one thing: when God brings you out of here, carry my bones with you.
And Genesis ends with this line: "and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." The book that began with a garden ends with a coffin in a foreign land, waiting to go home.
That's where chazak comes in. It means be strong. The tradition says it at the end of every one of the five books of the Torah, and it fits here most of all.

teach.h: YE MEANT EVIL; GOD MEANT IT FOR GOOD.
teach.b: Something long is finished. The ending isn't tidy. And the next book begins in slavery.
So before you turn the page: be strong, be strong, and strengthen each other.

how: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation stands and calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

o: a cheer of thanks to the person reading the Torah

games.q: you're Joseph. your father has died, and your brothers fall before you, afraid you'll finally take revenge. what do you do?
games.why: he weeps and says, "Fear not; for am I in the place of God?" and promises to care for them and their little ones.

practice: Look back at this part of the path: Rachel's grave, the coat, the pit, Tamar, the prison, the dreams, the cup, Judah, Ani Yosef, the grandsons. You finished it. Say the word, even quietly: chazak, be strong.

wordCard.voice: Chazak. Be strong. Called out in synagogue when a book of the Torah is finished: chazak, chazak, venitchazek.

orig.note: Hebrew: be strong. the same root describes the hardening of Pharaoh's heart later in Exodus.

carryVoice: Your line: be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. One whole book of the Torah, done.
